utterance: Hi Daniel, I'm Dr. Patel. I've got your booking for low back pain after a lift over the weekend. Thanks for coming in. Tell me from the start — what exactly happened, and what has your back been doing since?
reply: It happened on Saturday when I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden and felt a twinge, then I woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed, so it has been three days now. The pain is low down on the left side of my back, and sometimes it goes into my left buttock.

utterance:
Thanks, that helps. A few important questions to rule out anything more than a muscle or joint strain:

1. Does the pain go down past your knee into your leg, calf or foot, or does it stop around the buttock?
2. Any numbness, tingling, or weakness in your leg or foot — for example, trouble standing on your toes or heels, or your foot "giving way"?
3. Have you noticed anything with your bladder or bowels — difficulty starting a urine stream, leaking, constipation that's changed, or any numbness around your bottom, genitals or the area where you'd sit on a saddle?
reply: It stops around the buttock and doesn't go down my legs, my legs feel completely normal with no weakness or numbness, and everything with my bladder and bowels is all normal without any numbness around that area.

4. Have you had any fevers, night sweats, or lost weight recently without trying?

Your back looks like a mechanical muscle-and-joing strain: it's tender on the left side with some muscle spasm, your range of movement is limited by pain, but your spine bones are comfortable, your nerve tests in both legs are completely normal, and there are no warning signs of anything serious like a compression of the nerves at the base of the spine.

utterance:
So here's where things stand, and I want to be straight with you about the MRI.

Your examination is reassuring. The pain comes from a strained muscle on the left side of your lower back — the bones themselves aren't tender, your leg nerves are completely normal on both sides, and the specific warning signs we worry about — things like loss of bladder control, numbness around the bottom, or leg weakness — are all absent. In a situation like this, guidelines in Australia recommend against an MRI in the first six weeks, because scans this early often show harmless age-related changes that don't explain the pain, and they don't change what we'd do: rest it, take anti-inflammatories and get moving. I'm not going to refer you for an MRI today. If your pain is still not settling in four to six weeks, or if it starts shooting down a leg, that's the time to come back and we can reconsider imaging.

The plan:
1. Ibuprofen 400 mg, one tablet three times a day with food for five days. And paracetamol 1000 mg up to four times a day if you need it — the two can be taken together. I'm deliberately not using tramadol because of your allergy.
2. Please stop couch rest — complete bed rest actually makes these injuries last longer. Keep walking a little bit more each day, do your light household stuff, and bend and lift with your legs and keep things close in. Your heat pack is a good idea.
3. You can ease back into work at your own pace; a desk job is fine, just get up and walk every hour. Avoid heavy lifting for a couple of weeks.
4. If it's not clearly better in two to four weeks, come back and we can refer you for physiotherapy.

And the safety net — go to the emergency department the same day if you get any of these: trouble passing urine or loss of control, numbness around your bottom or genitals, new or worsening weakness in a leg, fever or shivering, or pain that's waking you at night and unexplained weight loss. Those would mean we need to look again urgently.

Does that make sense, and do you have any concerns about skipping the scan?
reply: Honestly? I've been reading about slipped discs and people needing surgery, so I am just worried this is serious and frustrated at being immobile.

awards.label: What he is worried the pain might be

utterance:
I completely understand why that's worrying — those internet stories are the small number of cases that need attention. But here's the reality: your pain stops at the buttock and your leg nerves test perfectly normal, so this looks like a muscle strain rather than a slipped disc pressing on a nerve. And even when a disc does slip, the overwhelming majority — well over 90% — heal on their own within a few weeks without any surgery. Surgery is only considered for people with steadily worsening leg weakness, or the emergency I mentioned — bladder problems with saddle numbness — and you have none of that.

Being "immobile" at day three is very common; the back muscles are in spasm and protecting themselves. The typical pattern is that the worst is over within about a week, and most people are back to normal within two to four weeks. Your pain score going down over the next few days will be the first sign it's working, and you can track that yourself.

So: the tablets, keep walking a bit each day, heat pack, and be kind to the back for a couple of weeks. I'd really encourage you to see improvement by two weeks — and if it's not, or if anything from that emergency list comes up, come straight back. I'd rather see you again than have you sit at home worrying.

Are you comfortable with that plan?
reply: I figured I'd need an MRI to see what's going on, but I suppose I can try these tablets and keep moving instead.
